title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is a system trained on copyrighted material without the rights holders' authorization. Udio, an AI music generation service, allegedly ingested large volumes of commercially released recordings to build models capable of producing new music in similar styles. The failure occurred at the training stage, before any user interaction, meaning the legal and ethical exposure was baked in from the beginning. Catching it would have required a licensing framework to be in place before training began, not after complaints arrived.

The incident produced multiple simultaneous legal fronts. Universal Music Group settled and moved toward a licensed platform. Warner Music Group reached a similar agreement. Sony Music filed a separate lawsuit alleging over 30,000 recordings were used without permission, and a class action brought by independent artists was allowed to proceed after a court declined to dismiss it. A musicians' union also brought claims related to the UMG settlement itself. The range of plaintiffs shows that the alleged harm extended across major labels, independent creators, and organized labor, not just a single rightsholder.

None of the lawsuits have produced final verdicts, and the allegations against Udio are not established findings. The settlement terms between Udio and Universal Music Group, and between Udio and Warner Music Group, remain undisclosed, so the financial consequences are not known from the available reporting.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, which had been accused of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system. Under the agreement, Udio will launch a new platform next year that uses only authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, and share songs. UMG's CEO stated the settlement demonstrates the company's commitment to supporting artists while embracing new technologies and developing innovative business models. Financial details of the settlement remain undisclosed.

The dispute centered on allegations that Udio used popular songs like The Temptations' "My Girl" to train its AI model, which then generated similar compositions without permission or payment. Udio had previously argued that AI learns from musical examples much like students studying music and scores. The company, launched in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, will compensate artists who opt into the new platform, though specifics were not provided. This marks Udio's first major licensing agreement with a major music label.
